title: From measurements to a finished garment: ease, yokes, bands

say: From measurements to a finished garment: ease, yokes and bands.
This is the video for module four of Advanced Knitting and Crochet.
Garments are where gauge, resizing and shaping come together. You start with a real body, and you choose ease on purpose. Ease is the difference between the body and the finished garment.
Then you calculate a top-down yoke, and finish with neat seams, bands and blocking. Good finishing can double what a customer is willing to pay.
A top needs ten measurements. Take the bust at the fullest part, with the tape level all round. Then waist, hip and back waist length.

Waist, hip and back waist length
Upper arm, wrist and arm length

say: Add cross back, armhole depth, upper arm, wrist, arm length, neck, and the garment length she wants.
Measure over light clothing, explain each one before you take it, and keep the card private. Write the date, because bodies change.

say: A close-fitting top has about 2.5 to 5 cm of ease at the bust.

panel.heading: How much ease at the bust?

cards.d: About 2.5 to 5 cm of ease. For fitted cardigans and tops.
About 5 to 10 cm of ease. For everyday jumpers and cardigans.
About 10 to 15 cm for relaxed tops, 15 cm or more for oversized cover-ups.

say: A standard fit has about 5 to 10 cm, for everyday jumpers.

say: Loose tops have about 10 to 15 cm, and oversized pieces 15 cm or more. Crochet stretches less than knitting, so many makers add a little more ease for crochet.

say: For example, Chioma in Asaba is knitting a standard-fitting jumper for a client with a 98 cm bust. She adds 8 cm of ease, for a finished bust of 106 cm. Front and back are 53 cm each.

panel.heading: Chioma turns a body into stitches
items: Draw it all on a schematic

say: Her gauge is 22 stitches per 10 cm, so 53 times 2.2 is 116.6. She rounds to 117 to suit her rib. The upper arm is 32 plus 4 cm of ease, 36 cm, which is 79 stitches.

panel.heading: Chioma turns a body into stitches
items: Draw it all on a schematic

say: She draws front, back and sleeve as simple shapes, and writes every number on them. That schematic is her plan and her check.

panel.heading: Chioma turns a body into stitches
items: Draw it all on a schematic
panel.rule: Finished measurement x stitches per cm = stitch count.

say: A top-down raglan starts at the neck. Four lines run to the underarms, and each increase round adds a stitch on both sides of each line, 8 stitches a round.
With a new yarn at 20 stitches per 10 cm, Chioma's 50 cm neck is 100 stitches: 34 back, 34 front, and 16 for each sleeve.

panel.heading: Calculating a seamless yoke
items: Sleeves need 24 rounds, then body only

say: The front must grow from 34 to 98 stitches. That is 64 more, 2 per round, so 32 increase rounds. The sleeves need only 24, so after 24 rounds she increases on the body only.

panel.heading: Calculating a seamless yoke
items: Sleeves need 24 rounds, then body only

say: With a plain round between increases, the yoke is about 23 cm deep. Before separating the sleeves, she slips the stitches onto a long cable and tries it on.

panel.heading: Calculating a seamless yoke
items: Sleeves need 24 rounds, then body only
panel.rule: Try the yoke on before you separate the sleeves.

say: Stitches are wider than rows are tall, so you cannot pick up one stitch per row. A common guide is 3 stitches for every 4 rows.
For example, Aisha in Ilorin has a 130-row edge. Her ratio is 22 divided by 30, about 0.73, so she needs about 95 stitches.

panel.heading: Aisha spaces six buttonholes
panel.rule: Pick up about 3 stitches for every 4 rows.

say: She wants 6 buttonholes of 2 stitches, with 3 stitches at each end. The stitches left over must divide by 5, the gaps between the holes. With 98 stitches, 80 are left, and 80 divided by 5 is 16.

panel.heading: Aisha spaces six buttonholes
panel.rule: Pick up about 3 stitches for every 4 rows.

say: She picks up 98 and spaces the holes 16 stitches apart. Then she checks the total adds back to 98.

panel.heading: Aisha spaces six buttonholes
panel.rule: Pick up about 3 stitches for every 4 rows.

say: Weave in ends with tails of at least 15 cm, then block. Cotton and viscose stretch when wet, so dry them flat, never hanging.

cards.d: Wet block. They stretch when wet and heavy, so dry flat, never hanging.
Wet or steam block. No hot water with rubbing, or it can felt and shrink.
Never press with a hot iron. Hold steam above, keep hands clear, switch off at the wall.

say: Wool can be wet or steam blocked, but hot water with rubbing makes it felt and shrink.

cards.d: Wet block. They stretch when wet and heavy, so dry flat, never hanging.

say: Never press acrylic with a hot iron. Steam can scald, so hold the iron above the fabric, keep your hands clear, keep it away from children, and switch it off at the wall when you finish.
Pin each piece to your schematic and add a care label.

say: To remember. Choose ease on purpose. Finished size times gauge gives your stitches. Each raglan increase round adds 8 stitches. Pick up about 3 stitches for every 4 rows. And block by fibre, using steam with care.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Block by fibre; steam with care

say: Now make a measurement card and schematic, calculate your own raglan with every check shown, and finish a sample band with three evenly spaced buttonholes and a care label.
